subtopic: STEPS TO DEAL WITH SEASONAL UNEMPLOYMENT DURING COMING WINTER

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: STEPS TO DEAL WITH SEASONAL UNEMPLOYMENT DURING COMING WINTER
speechtext:
Although it is early summer, I should like to make a statement concerning the government's programs to attack seasonal unemployment next winter. While the employment situation has improved over the past year, the problem of seasonal unemployment will be with us again next winter. An announcement of the government's measures to increase winter employment is desirable at this time so as to allow municipalities and the construction industry adequate time to engage in advance planning.
The municipal winter works incentive program which has been so successful in providing additional winter employment at the local level will be continued next winter. The winter house building incentive program, introduced on an experimental basis last winter, was successful beyond all expectations. It will be carried out again during the winter of 1964-65.
Every effort will be made to improve the effectiveness of both the municipal winter works incentive program and the winter house building incentive program for the coming winter, and any modifications which may be desirable in this connection will be announced at a later date. The basic principles on which both these programs operate, however, will not be modified.

subtopic: STEPS TO DEAL WITH SEASONAL UNEMPLOYMENT DURING COMING WINTER
speechtext:
We are happy to hear that the government intends to continue these programs, particularly the municipal winter works program which was started in 1958-59 and which has met with tremendous success year after year. The municipalities have become increasingly aware

Labour Conditions
of the value of this program and are participating more actively each and every winter. As time goes on many more projects are being undertaken under this plan.
We are glad the government have decided to carry it on, and I hope they will continue to expand it in order to help those who would otherwise be seasonally unemployed. I might say in passing that the Secretary of State for External Affairs was one of those who disagreed with this program, but now he is smiling; he is happy about it because it has proved successful.
As far as the house building program is concerned, after only one winter's experience it has yet to be seen whether it will continue its impetus, and we look forward with interest to seeing whether this program will expand or whether it has been only a flash in the pan.

subtopic: STEPS TO DEAL WITH SEASONAL UNEMPLOYMENT DURING COMING WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we greatly appreciate the statement just made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) and the assurance he has given to municipalities and provinces to the effect that the winter works program will be continued and also his intention to increase the assistance provided to stir up housing construction during winter.
However, I should like to call the Minister of Labour's attention to certain conditions prevailing in some areas of our country, so that he may reconsider his decision to curtail the winter works period in the so-called designated areas or in those where severe weather conditions make it practically impossible to carry out some winter works.
I should like also to suggest to the minister that, among the projects that the municipalities can undertake under the provisions of the act concerning winter works incentives, there is the construction of buildings which could be rented by municipalities to small enterprises and secondary industries which cannot themselves put capital in the construction of large buildings. I know that certain municipalities consider erecting buildings which could be rented to agencies and small companies in the province of Quebec and throughout Canada which can produce nothing now but would then be able to produce. I believe that this would help designated areas by giving work to the available manpower and creating employment which could not exist otherwise.
I know that during the winter works period just terminated Quebec received a large share

of the amounts made available to the provinces. We are glad to see that for once a piece of legislation permits Quebec to obtain benefits it has never known before.
I commend the government for it, but I must also admit that this legislation had been first introduced by the previous government. It is a good piece of legislation which helps to alleviate unemployment, but we find that unemployment is still our main concern, especially in the province of Quebec where, according to the latest statistics, the largest number of unemployed persons, that is 38 per cent, is to be found.
I think the government, in co-operation with the Quebec government and the municipalities, should find some other solution to improve a situation which is unfavourable to our province, for it is largely responsible for the present difficulties and discontent. I hope the government will take advantage of the summer period to prepare programs to be announced in the fall and which will tend to markedly reduce unemployment.

subtopic: STEPS TO DEAL WITH SEASONAL UNEMPLOYMENT DURING COMING WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course, the winter works program supplies jobs for the unemployed during the most difficult period.
However, I wonder if the government deserves congratulations or should be made the butt of ridicule, because during the winter works period, steam shovels and bulldozers are left in heated garages or on parking lots, and while the temperature is often 20 or 30 below zero, men are employed on outside work; they have to dig for sewer systems and water works when the ground is frozen. That goes against common sense, against progress.
Mr. Speaker, I remind the government that it would now be possible to find other solutions to unemployment without compelling individuals to work in ditches in winter, when it is very cold, while tractors and steam shovels are left in heated garages.
We should try and find another method, another system; but under our absurd system, I admit that the Minister of Labour could not find another solution to get the men to work. Nevertheless, improvements should be made, as the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) said a while ago.
Last year, we of the Ralliement Creditiste exerted pressures in order to have the winter works period extended in places where the weather is the most severe, so that they could enjoy the advantages provided by the legislation.

subtopic: STEPS TO DEAL WITH SEASONAL UNEMPLOYMENT DURING COMING WINTER
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: STEPS TO DEAL WITH SEASONAL UNEMPLOYMENT DURING COMING WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I heard the hon. member for Port Arthur say "carried." I wish to draw to your attention the fact that when it is time to discuss western wheat many hon. members endlessly take the floor and we bear with them, because it is a problem with which their region is faced.
On the other hand, the hon. member for Port Arthur is always discussing problems which do not interest us and we do not interrupt him. Therefore, he should grant us the privilege to deal with the problems we are interested in.

subtopic: STEPS TO DEAL WITH SEASONAL UNEMPLOYMENT DURING COMING WINTER
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: STEPS TO DEAL WITH SEASONAL UNEMPLOYMENT DURING COMING WINTER
speechtext:
Another observation, Mr. Speaker. The salary of those who carry out winter works is not the same all across the country. In fact, in certain regions or localities it varies from $2 to $2.25 per hour, while in some other places it is $1, $1.15 and $1.25 per hour.
I think that in setting the winter works period for next year, the minister should take steps to standardize the salary all across the country, so that everybody can earn a reasonable pay, that is $2 or $2.25 per hour.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago the Leader of the Opposition asked a question about the transfer of employees of the Canadian Commercial Corporation to the Department of Industry, and I said that inquiries had been made into the circumstances surrounding that matter. subtopic: TRANSFER OF EMPLOYEES TO DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY
speechtext: Revert to motions.

subtopic: TRANSFER OF EMPLOYEES TO DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
When employees of an exempt agency are transferred to a department or agency which is subject to the Civil
Inquiries of the Ministry Service Act, the civil service commission is required under that act to determine the classification and grade for which those employees are qualified. This procedure was followed in connection with the transfer of employees of the Canadian Commercial Corporation to the Department of Industry. The government has decided that where a function and staff are transferred in this way, the employees concerned should not suffer a reduction in salary. Employees who are rated by the civil service commission in classifications having a lesser salary will be paid their former rate of pay until such time as the rate attaching to the classification in which they are being certified becomes equal to that former rate.
In line with this policy the employees of the Canadian Commercial Corporation transferred to the Department of Industry who are filling positions at classifications for which the rate of pay is lower than the rate paid by the corporation will be paid on transfer at their former rate. As hon. members will have seen, a number of the employees who would be affected by this policy have appealed to the civil service commission against the classification they have been given, and the effect of the new policy in each of these cases will naturally depend on the outcome of the appeal.

subtopic: JOINT PARTICIPATION IN CELEBRATION BY CANADA AND U.S.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: JOINT PARTICIPATION IN CELEBRATION BY CANADA AND U.S.
speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Secretary of State. Has the hon. gentleman any information he can give the house with respect to legislation coming before the Senate of the United States which will provide for joint participation by the United States and Canada in the 1967 centenary celebrations?

subtopic: JOINT PARTICIPATION IN CELEBRATION BY CANADA AND U.S.
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker.

May I briefly recapitulate the points I was making yesterday before the committee adjourned at ten o'clock. I said then that I had no complaint whatever to make about the minister or his staff with respect to the way in which they dealt with individual cases brought to their attention. My quarrel was with the system which I described-and I did so deliberately-as a rotten system.
In my view that strong expression of opinion is justified for this reason. Parliament has in fact, contrary I suggest to what the minister said or implied, conferred on prospective immigrants a statutory right. This is not a statutory right to enter the country absolutely, but it is a statutory right under the act to the benefit of a hearing to determine whether they are admissible in accordance with the standards set out in the act and the regulations. This statutory right is denied in practice. The reasons which are given for denying the right to a hearing are meaningless; statements such as "You do not have a visa". Of course the only authority which can grant a visa is the department itself, and the department has already refused to give a visa, and refused, also, to give any reason for withholding a visa.
The minister told the committee that he is getting advice as to immigration procedure from an eminent lawyer, Mr. Sedgwick. That is all very well. I do not complain about it; I think Mr. Sedgwick could be helpful. But let me say this to the minister. We have absolutely no need of an eminent lawyer to discover that a hearing without disclosure of the real grounds for rejection is practically meaningless; it is not, in fact, a fair hearing. There are plenty of lawyers on both sides of this house who are perfectly capable of informing the minister of the elementary principle involved, which is this. Before any important question affecting the rights of an individual is determined, that individual

should have the right to be heard, and this means knowing why he is being denied the right he is seeking.
This is an elementary principle of justice, and there are dozens of cases to support my contention. As I say, we need not go outside this house, or beyond the lawyers who sit on the hon. gentleman's side of the house, to find that this principle has long been recognized. The courts have made it abundantly clear. As long ago as 1932 Mr. Justice Duff in a supreme court case described immigration proceedings with which he was dealing as "hugger-mugger". Mr. Justice Rand, in the Supreme Court of Canada and Mr. Justice Aylesworth in the Brent case, in the court of appeal, as I recall it, described similar proceedings as farcical.
This farcical procedure, this "hugger-mugger", is still going on. Indeed, it is the standard procedure in immigration matters. It negates the bill of rights. The bill of rights says that no act of parliament shall be construed or applied so as to deprive a person of the right of a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations. This solemn undertaking made by parliament and given to the people of Canada is flouted almost daily in immigration proceedings as a result of which people seeking to exercise a statutory right to come to Canada- if they can comply with the standards of admission-are deported on meaningless grounds after a mere parade of words which conceals the real reason for rejection.
I know there is a reason for this, but I suggest to the minister and the committee that it is not an adequate reason. The basis is said to be the need for security, and it is contended that in many of these cases reasons for non-admission cannot be disclosed without breaking faith with some outside source. I say to the minister, what crimes are committed in the name of security; what unjust, misleading lists of so-called subversives have been compiled on the basis of gossip, malice and sheer stupidity. I suggest that if there are security reasons for refusing, for example, a son in Canada the right to bring his parents to this country, or parents the right to bring their children, or a husband the right to have his wife join him here, such grounds should be carefully scrutinized by an independent judicial tribunal having full access to all the facts available to the department. Nothing short of such a full review will refute the belief that security reasons are
Interim Supply
sometimes advanced as a smokescreen to hide less creditable motives.
What do I suggest is the remedy? I recognize it is not enough simply to complain about the administration of this act and its regulations. First of all, I say there is no one remedy. The first step toward a remedy is that the department should decide in all cases except where serious security questions are in issue to disclose fully the real reasons for refusal of admission.
I say that I am personally acquainted with cases in which the real reason for refusal of admission was totally different from that advanced in the formal record, yet had nothing whatever to do with security reasons when it was looked into. Let the department decide, without getting the advice of eminent lawyers, to make fuller disclosure of the reasons. Let it take the advice of members of the house, for example, and decide that it will disclose these things more fully.
Second, I suggest that an independent judicial review of an administrative nature is required in all cases of refusal of admission. The appeal board should be given full access to the real reasons for rejection, and they should be given the power to recommend clemency or suspension of the full letter of the law on compassionate grounds.
Third, I suggest there should be a parliamentary committee charged with the responsibility of reviewing the immigration laws and regulations and their administration. I believe it is this parliament that has the primary responsibility for ensuring that the laws it makes are applied with fairness and justice to those who seek to come to Canada, and I urge that such a parliamentary committee, if no appropriate committee exists, be established not just to examine this matter now but to carry on a review throughout the years. I suggest that this will relieve succeeding ministers from the frequent embarrassment to which they are subject when parliament does not have an established right to look into these matters.
Fourth, I recommend that there should be something in the nature of an immigration ombudsman, if I may use that term, some independent parliamentary commissioner who would be able to advise both members of parliament and individuals, who would have full access to immigration records. In cases where in his judgment he thought there was some unfairness or injustice produced, he would have the duty of reporting to parliament.

Interim Supply
Lastly, Mr. Chairman, the minister needs no eminent counsel to advise him that the traces of discrimination that remain in the act and the regulations should be removed. These overt references to discrimination on racial grounds should be wiped out. The house will recall that in the past the act and the regulations clearly and explicitly referred to discrimination on racial grounds as a basis of Canadian policy. Fortunately most of that has disappeared, but I have called the attention of the house and the minister to the fact that sections remain which deal specifically with this form of discrimination. I give as an example section 61, I think it is, of the Immigration Act. I have introduced a private members' bill, No. C-69, which will not be reached during this session. I would not feel badly at all if the minister would say he would take the onus of removing this section from the Immigration Act which refers specifically to racial discrimination.
On this score I recommend that the minister should take another look at regulation 31. This is the main regulation dealing with the admission of relatives, and I urge him to see whether it cannot be amended so there will be no explicit discrimination in the regulations. I remind the house and the minister that there is one section which imposes harsh and narrow standards for the admission of people who come from Asia or Africa but far more liberal standards of admission for those who come from Europe or America. In the world as we have it today I do not believe there is any room for this continuing discrimination on geographical or on racial grounds.
I cannot leave this subject without expressing the hope that we can change the immigration administration so that no one can be expelled without the reasons therefor being given. Let us make sure that the will of parliament as expressed in the Immigration Act is not flouted from day to day and that the principles of natural justice, which are familiar to every member of the house, are brought into play in the daily administration of these regulations. I believe this would then predispose immigration officers to treat immigrants as though they were persons with rights.
I have heard too often that these people have no rights. They have rights. Parliament has given them rights. As long as these rights are flouted in practice the officers themselves can hardly be blamed for treating these people as though they do not matter very much and in some cases, for example, letting them

languish in jail beyond any reasonable time. I suggest that what is basically important is that we recognize that these people who come from various parts of the world are human beings who are entitled to be treated with dignity as human beings.
I want to close by saying to the minister that many ministers have struggled with the problem of the Immigration Act and regulations. He is by no means the first to do this. Many of them have made promises as to what they were going to do and how they were going to change everything. I say the minister has a wonderful opportunity to score a real break-through in this area, a break-through that has eluded his predecessors.
I do not particularly think the advice of eminent lawyers is what is required. I think a basic change of heart and a recognition of the rights of these immigrants are what is in issue. Therefore I have refrained and intend to continue to refrain from hurling insults and criticisms at the minister himself, but I say to him that I hope he will take the opportunity that is his to make a real breakthrough in this regard so that Canadians can be proud of their immigration laws and can hold their heads high anywhere in the world when discussing immigration matters.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take much of the time of the committee now, as I understand the estimates of the department will be coming forward in the very near future. However, I do want to make a few remarks on the general topic of immigration and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. First of all I want to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Greenwood on the remarks he has made today. I certainly wish to associate myself with what he has said and the remedies he has suggested to the committee.
One of the most frustrating things that a member of parliament or any individual dealing with immigration matters encounters is not being able to obtain the reasons for a person being refused admission to the country. Perhaps there are logical reasons for this stand, but to date I have not been able to find out why this position is taken. As the hon. member for Greenwood has stated, on many occasions the only reason given is security. What does "security" mean? It is a nebulous term unless it is defined, unless we are made aware of what are the security reasons and what precautions are being taken.

At the present time the security reason is not known. It is very difficult to explain to a sponsor who comes to your office that his son or daughter and son in law have been refused admission on security grounds. I say to the minister that this matter has to be reviewed very carefully because the word "security" alone is not sufficient.
Dealing with general immigration practice, Mr. Chairman, I would point out that some three years ago it was decided that the emphasis with regard to immigration would be placed on those with skills and education, and I think this is good. However, this policy is being interpreted in too restrictive a manner. It is being used as a disguise and smokescreen to justify the refusal of immigrants who wish to come to this country. It is too restrictive.
A sponsor who wants to bring his son or daughter or orphan nephew to this country receives a form letter from the department saying they do not meet the requirements of the Immigration Act, and therefore consideration cannot be given at this time to allowing so and so to enter the country. These are the only reasons given, and I think it is time this policy was reviewed. There is a growing recognition that Canada's immigration facilities are inadequate, and we certainly want more immigrants who will become Canadian citizens. In the 1960's, as in the 1860's, Canada is the most underpopulated country in the world, yet we encompass a greater land area than any other nation except perhaps the U.S.S.R. If the minister really wants a more ambitious program to attract the kind of skilled immigrants we need, then we will have to take off our kid gloves and fight a strong battle with our most active competitors, especially Australia and South Africa.
If the present economic expansion should be slowed down for the lack of skilled workers, many economists state that the unskilled workers will suffer. The decision three years ago by the previous Conservative government to put the immigration emphasis on skills rather than race or country has placed Canada in direct competition with other nations. No longer do the skilled people migrate from Britain or Europe out of desperation or fear. Europe today has a generally high standard of employment and living. Canada's continuing policy "If you want to come", is not good enough for today. The people from Britain and western Europe have
Interim Supply
to be wooed and won. The skilled people in Europe are remaining in Europe today.
I must compliment the minister on a recent speech he made in which he stated:
We need an active immigration policy, better facilities, better personnel, more personnel, more contact with other governments and more publicity.
I could not agree more with this statement, Mr. Chairman. I doubt if the department, as it is presently constituted, can launch an aggressive, active program to obtain more immigrants. We have some 32 offices abroad staffed by some 350 people. This is a ridiculous number of people to be staffing these offices. In my opinion there are not enough offices. Perhaps the minister's remarks portend a greater activity in this field.
We have heard a great deal, Mr. Chairman, about changes in the Immigration Act and in immigration regulations. In my opinion the biggest sin in our immigration policy today is that it is being dealt with by regulation rather than by an act. We need a sound Immigration Act to which we can look for enforcement, to which we can look for an aggressive policy of immigration. We should be able to look to the Immigration Act and say, this is our immigration policy. The regulations are really only a smokescreen, as the hon. member for Greenwood said.
The regulations leave too much to the discretion of departmental officials, not only those abroad but those in Canada today. There is too much power in the hands of departmental officials because there is vagueness in the regulations. Vagueness breeds power and, so far as I am concerned, vagueness breeds all kinds of definitions which cannot be pinned down. The time has come, therefore, when there should be an overhaul of our Immigration Act and regulations. I am not one who believes in immigration policy by regulation. We can only benefit from a liberalization of our immigration policy. Newcomers influence our economy in many, many ways. They contribute to manpower. They participate in establishing new industries. In fact they promote employment for Canadian workers and many times they repopulate our farms. They become important consumers who bring with them immense sums of capital and personal effects.
I should like to deal very briefly with the problem of Chinese immigration from Hong Kong. I hope the minister will be able to answer these questions. I understand that

Interim Supply
immigration offices have been opened in Cairo and Beirut. I have nothing against immigration from these two parts of the world, and presumably there were good reasons for the opening of these offices. However, in 1962 only 964 immigrants came from Egypt and 292 from Lebanon. We have offices in other countries such as Italy, France where we have two, Hong Kong. I do not believe we have sufficient staff in Italy where we only have the one office in Rome. So far as I am concerned this is a disgraceful situation, not only because the department cannot handle the volume of applicants but because the applicants cannot be examined. Surely in a country from which there is a great volume of immigrants we should have better facilities, more personnel and at least two offices, one for the northern part of the country and one for the southern part.
We know the discrimination that has been practised in Hong Kong. The minister, in his speech yesterday, mentioned the organization of many rackets for illegal entry of immigrants. This is not more prevalent anywhere than in Hong Kong today or in the past few years. The Chinese people have had a problem, and I feel that problem is one that we have created. There is a great backlog of applicants in Hong Kong. No one knows what happens to these applicants. I have had ex-erience with many of them, and when the sponsors in Canada make application for these people in Hong Kong, sometimes these people are not heard from for a year or longer. The representatives of the Chinese community submitted a brief to the former minister of citizenship and immigration, now the Minister of Justice, in which they requested improvements in the machinery for admitting their relatives to Canada. They have suggested various remedies, one of which was the establishment of an independent tribunal, as mentioned by the hon. member for Greenwood. This independent tribunal would verify the bona fides of the Chinese immigrants.
This brief suggested also the admittance of sons and daughters of Chinese Canadian residents irrespective of age or marital status; the elimination of existing delays in the applications of sponsored relatives; the discontinuance of the prosecution of Chinese for past illegal entries into Canada. I am happy to say that as soon as this government took office this practice, established by the former administration, was eliminated.

I wonder if the hon. member will permit a question.
[Mr. Macaluso.l

I will as soon as I am finished. Our immigration, not only from Hong Kong but from Great Britain and all other countries, has been most unsatisfactory for several years. I wonder at times what is wrong. Is our immigration geared to bringing people in or keeping them out? I wonder at times, Mr. Chairman, why we speak very actively and very aggressively about immigration, but we really have not done too much about it over the past 10 or 15 years. I believe the last year in which there was active immigration was right after the war and in 1956 after the Hungarian uprising. Since that time we have not done too much about it. Our staffs are poorly paid; the personnel is not too strong. I sincerely ask the minister, when he is reviewing policy, to deal with these matters as soon as possible in order to alleviate this backlog of applications.
I should like to mention one other matter, Mr. Chairman; the Canadian citizenship courts. I believe this was a policy the former government established, and it was a good policy. I believe that today the immigrant who goes to one of these courts to obtain his certificate of citizenship, receives it with pride. I should like to mention the ceremonies that are performed by the court president and the great job that is done in the city of Hamilton by the I.O.D.E. in their reception for these people after the ceremonies, and by the city officials themselves. I know that they felt more pride in becoming citizens of this country. However, I believe the minister should very actively review the questions that are being asked by some of the citizenship court presidents. When immigrants go to fill out their applications for Canadian certificates of citizenship and are examined, many of the examinations are held in camera. Applicants at times are very nervous, and they are asked certain questions by the president of the citizenship court. Because of a lack of complete understanding of the language they may be at a disadvantage.
This is something I have discussed with the minister on many occasions. I have also talked about it with some other hon. members on this side of the chamber, and we are agreed there is no uniformity in the examination of applicants for citizenship papers. This is something that causes hardship. When I am in my offices at home people come and ask me why they have been refused citizenship, and tell me they have been remanded for one or two years. The explanation is simple. A person must have an understanding of the

English or French language, and this is only right. It is very difficult to obtain employment in this country if one does not have an understanding of the languages of the country, and sometimes of the geography of the country.
On occasion applicants have been asked how many square miles there are in Canada, what is the largest or smallest river, and who is the lieutenant governor of B.C. These are questions which are asked of people in Hamilton. They are unfair questions; many of us could not answer them ourselves. I urge the minister to see to it that there is some form of uniform examination, and I suggest that a booklet be prepared and sent to citizenship court presidents outlining procedures for a uniform examination.
I do not say this is the case with all the presidents of the courts. I know of instances where excellent examinations are conducted, but I also know of cases where the examinations are not just or equitable. When he is summing up later on I hope the minister will outline what he intends to do regarding citizenship court presidents and our offices abroad.
I now turn to another matter. The policy of the Liberal party in the general elections of 1962 and 1963 called for an appeal tribunal to be set up. I quote from that policy:
Decisions of immigration officials will be subject to review by appropriate and independent tribunals.
I urge the minister to advise the committee when this policy will be implemented. I shall now accept the question from the hon. member for Bow River.

The question is a short one. Is it not a fact that during the time hon. Mrs. Fairclough was minister of citizenship and immigration the regulations were changed which affect the Chinese and other people from that area? Is not that a fair comment in that regard?

No, Mr. Chairman, I say it is not a fair comment in that regard. I do not say this critically, but at no time were the regulations affecting the Chinese alleviated; let us put it that way. In fact it was the opposite. At no time was there more action to deport Chinese citizens who came in illegally. This is not a criticism, because I believe it was the duty of the departmental officials to concern themselves with those who came into the country illegally. I do not make any criticism of that policy, but I do not follow the hon. member for Bow River
Interim. Supply
when he says the regulations were changed. Perhaps they may have been.

I do not want to make a speech at this time, but if the hon. member will check Hansard he will see that the regulations affecting the Chinese and other people from that area were changed so they were given equal status in coming to Canada with people from other lands. Whether the departmental officials started to implement that immediately might be another question, but I say to the hon. member that if he checks Hansard he will find the regulations, in fact and by number, were changed so they were given equal status with people coming from Europe and other lands.

I will say this; I agree the
regulations were changed so that the qualification regarding race and country of origin was thrown out and the emphasis was placed on education and skills. As I stated previously, the interpretations of these regulations is being used as a smokescreen. The hon. member and I are not in disagreement, but there is ministerial discretion even in that case, and this applies to all ministers who have held the citizenship portfolio. The regulation was made uniform regarding education and skills, but there is still discrimination in the regulations, and when you examine section 31 you find this discrimination is still practised in the department or by some officials.
I repeat that Canada today needs skilled people, educated people, but we are finding it more and more difficult to compete and we need an aggressive policy in order to take advantage of that situation.

Mr. Chairman, it is 11 days since debate on interim supply started. At that time I opened up on the subject of citizenship and immigration and said many people had spent a lot of time in jail without legal justification, without excuse, and apparently without enough attention being paid by the minister. The attitude has changed slightly since then, in that now we have the appointment of Mr. Sedgwick, who is going to inquire into some of these matters.

Even if the program greatly alleviates unemployment, it does have serious disadvantages. In brief, let us say that the winter works, as they are carried out now, affect the farmers in the first place by gradual increases of real estate taxes, to such an extent that farmers who succeeded in making a living, a few years ago, are now leaving our rural regions. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member knows that he cannot reflect upon a vote of the house. I am not saying that the whole substance of his speech is out of order, but certainly when he refers to a particular incident on which a vote of the house was taken I would think that he is reflecting on that vote. This is the suggestion I make. The hon. member, I know, will want to take that into consideration.

I would want to take cognizance of your ruling and stay within your ruling. I want to say this: I was not reflecting on any vote of the house. I was reflecting on certain circumstances which took place before the vote.
However, I will move along now because I do not want to have a red herring drawn over my speech. I want to lay down the facts and bring them before the members of this house. In my opinion, as a member of this house, the Prime Minister has misled the house. I have read two statements and I want to read another. I quote from page 3836 of Hansard for June 2, 1964, and the reference is to this same subject. The Prime Minister was asked by the hon. member for Yukon, a certain question and this was his reply:
I did not see it in my office. I saw it in Toronto at a studio, and it was shown in an office in the east block. I saw part of it there but the sound track was so bad I left after a few minutes because it could not be understood.
Then the hon. member for Pontiac-Temisca-mingue asked a supplementary question as follows:
I have a question supplementary to the previous question asked of the Prime Minister. I was wondering if, as a sophisticated critic of art, he would tell us what he thought of the film "Mr. Pearson" when he saw it?
I found it exceedingly interesting, Mr. Speaker.

Revealing?

Interim Supply
It is revealing; it is revealing that they will not come forward and tell the facts in this house when they are asked for the facts.
Let us consider another story, an independent story for a few moments. I should like now to turn to another set of facts that took place on June 15, 1964. I emphasize again that if we, as members of parliament, irrespective of the side of the house on which we sit, endorse what is going on now on the front benches of this government, parliament will come into such disrespect it will take years for parliament to regain its importance in our land.
What about five or six years ago?

My friend is inquiring about six years ago; he left out two years, and I suppose he is talking about the pipe line debate. It is still haunting him.
Let me go back to the facts. I should like to quote from page 4329 of Hansard for June 15, 1964, a speech by the Leader of the Opposition:
When the Prime Minister indulged in quotations he did not think of bringing to the attention of the house the letter he received from the various intellectuals who signed that message on May 27.
In order that the record will be clear, I should say that the letter was from a group of intellectuals in this country with reference to the flag. The Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, X received no such letter.
I am going to lay the groundwork for the statement that again the Prime Minister did not tell the facts and the truth in this house.
Oh, oh.

I know; I feel the same way. On May 27, there was a letter written and signed by various intellectuals in this country. One of those intellectuals was Denis Smith, assistant to the president and assistant professor of politics, Trent University, Peterborough. This letter was dated May 27, 1964.
I am now going to read from page 4330 of Hansard. Why does the Prime Minister want to hide these things? What is he afraid of? Why is he afraid of this film? Is he afraid because of the fake build-up of images in another land? Is he afraid because he has been told images have proven to be very important in political life? Well, if this image crosses the land then the people of Canada will find out what goes on in this government, and particularly what comes from the mouth of the Prime Minister.

At page 4330 he is recorded as saying that he would not like to mislead the house.
I received no such letter but I did get a letter on my desk. It was addressed "Dear Mr. ..." blank, and there was no signature to it, but it had that body.
I suggest that the Prime Minister did receive a letter dated May 27, 1964, and that it was not addressed to his blank office, because his office is not blank at the moment. It was addressed "The Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, P.C., M.P., Prime Minister of Canada, Ottawa, Ontario" and it began "Dear Mr. Prime Minister". The letter had on it the names of various people, one of whom was the assistant to the president and assistant professor of political science at Trent University, Peterborough, a Mr. Denis Smith.
Why did the Prime Minister say it was not directed to him? Why did he say it was addressed "Dear Mr. . . ." blank? Did he want to tell the house that he had not received a letter from the intellectuals criticizing the flag which his government is bringing in, and which the hon. member for Royal said last night is a manufactured issue to cover up the irresponsibility, inadequacy and inefficiency of the government?
Those are the two points I want to make and I have made them. First of all the facts in reference to the questions on the film were not true, and he has not told us the facts in reference to the flag.
I could bring up another matter, but I do not have time to quote upon it. When this house first met after October of 1963, I asked the Prime Minister about the winter games in Banff. He said that the Department of External Affairs sent officials and one important minister to a conference; but later, when I placed the question on the order paper, I got a written reply stating there were no officials sent and the answer from the minister, which was different from that by the Prime Minister, was to the effect that it was against the law to send them; that it was not a conference but a committee. And so the Prime Minister sneaked out the back door instead of the front door in discussing that problem.
I say this, respecting the office of the Prime Minister, that the Prime Minister who gave that answer knew no officials of the Department of External Affairs were at that winter games meeting, whether it was a conference, a committee or whatever it was.
Having gone that far, and certainly I have gone far, I would say to him that he should take and reread something that should haunt the government and himself because of these discrepancies which I have set out, and on

which he sat silently and failed to speak on a most important point of privilege. I may add there were many shocked people on the government back benches yesterday, as there were on this side of the house, when the Prime Minister remained silent and refused to answer. But what he should do is reread what he said in this chamber on February 4, 1963, when he wanted an election, when the Liberals were hungry for power. This is what he said in reference to our leader:
We face emergencies and problems in this country at this time. We need a government that will make decisions-
Then he went on:
He must have felt very sad-
Hear, hear.

You can clap now as much as you like, but when I come to the section you don't like you won't be clapping.
He must have felt very sad in making the kind of speech he had to make, but at that time he said, quoting the immortal words of Cromwell when he went into the Long Parliament:
"You have sat here too long for the little good that you have been doing.
Then, after some interruption, he finished the quotation:
Depart, I say, and let's have done with you. In God's name, go."
I say to the Prime Minister, who is not here now, what he said to the former prime minister, "in God's name, go."
That is not what they said yesterday.

I say this, according to the natural law, according to the law of wisdom, according to the divine law, the law of God, this Prime Minister should leave because he is misinforming and misrepresenting facts in this House of Commons; and if he knows his responsibility he will leave.
I can only believe, when someone said he was steeped in the fine arts, that he might have been steeped in the fine arts of diplomacy. I believe most people will accept that, but maybe he read too seriously and got his two positions he has held mixed up, because I quote from page 452 of Plato's work, "The Republic", where the author discusses diplomacy:
The rulers of the state are the only ones who should have the privilege of lying, either at home or abroad; they may be allowed to lie for the good of the state.
We know what Plato meant, when you are dealing with external affairs; but when we are dealing with the business of the House 20220-294

of Commons and the business of the Canadian people then I say to you, Mr. Chairman, it is a different situation.
The Prime Minister remains silent. The words were read while he was here in the chamber and they showed he said, '1 did not see that film." If he had been allowed to answer again we would probably have received another version; but I must not digress because it is important. That is the charge I make against the Prime Minister. I say it is a serious charge and I have documented the statements I have made. Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up any more time of the committee.

As I listened to the hon. member for Bow River certain things struck me very strongly. A serious charge was made against the Prime Minister, which was a reiteration of a point of privilege brought up yesterday. I thing it is high time it did.
There is another point which is very germane, and that is all this laughing which is going on, on the Liberal side. I and many people across Canada think they are well equipped to sit down and laugh but they cannot get up and talk any sense.
There is another matter I would like to mention-that the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle was expelled from this house-that is the only word I can use-as a result of statements which he made as to the facts which the Prime Minister of this country had put before the house.

What a contribution.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal with a subject which interests more particularly the farmers of the province of Quebec. A large number of farmers including pipe, cigar and cigarette tobacco growers,
[The Deputy Chairman.]
are concerned at the present time because they have no protection against crop damage by hail or frost.
The federal government has drawn up a bill which should be very beneficial to farmers if, of course, the interested provinces will sign an agreement with Ottawa to avail themselves of such benefits.
In 1961, I wrote to the provincial minister of agriculture, Hon. Alcide Courcy, to ask him what were the intentions of the provincial government in this regard, so that the government could decide whether or not to take advantage of this crop insurance legislation.
I am happy to read to the house part of the reply dated July 24, 1961, from the provincial minister of agriculture:
Dear Sir: In reply to your letter of June 14,
I can assure you that the provincial government intends, in principle, to take advantage of the federal Crop Insurance Act to the extent that the people primarily interested, that is the agricultural producers, will want to take advantage of it.
Mr. Chairman, there is no doubt that farmers who go in for special crops need the protection offered by the Crop Insurance Act.
Recently again, in Joliette, a storm swept through several farms where cigarette tobacco is grown. Losses amounted to thousands of dollars. If, in 1961, the Quebec government had signed an agreement with Ottawa, the owners of those farms would have been protected and could have received the money needed to recoup their losses.
Again I ask the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), who unfortunately is not in the house, as well as the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and a great number of ministers-
You should know that he is in hospital.
I take this opportunity to ask the Secretary of State, who gets along so well with the authorities of the province of Quebec-
That is true.

-including Mr. Rene Levesque, to urge the Quebec government to sign an agreement so as to protect the farmers of that province, especially those who go in for special farming, such as the tobacco growers.
The average income of eastern farmers, that is, of Quebec farmers, is approximately $1,200 a year. I know, Mr. Chairman, that a few provinces have already entered into an agreement with the federal government so as to benefit from the Crop Insurance Act. It would be essential, in my opinion, that the Quebec

Interim Supply
government should sign this agreement without delay and start by extending this act to tobacco growers, and then to fruit and vegetable growers, in order to cover eventually all Quebec farmers.
Mr. Chairman, this is what I had to say and I hope that the federal government and the Minister of Agriculture, as well as the Minister of Forestry, who is unfortunately absent from the house, will do their best in this connection.
I hope that some other minister will tell them to meet with Hon. Alcide Courcy- we all know that the federal Minister of Agriculture is on excellent terms with the provincial minister of agriculture-to ask him to co-operate as soon as possible with Ottawa in the best interests of Quebec agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, during the next few minutes, I should like to express the views of the average worker in Quebec and throughout Canada concerning the way the government of the day is handling the affairs of our country.
May I say that workers, who are commonly called average citizens, have lost all confidence in the present Liberal administration. Considering the numerous promises which were made during the 1962 and 1963 election campaigns, they had a right to expect that things would be a lot better than they are at present. After having trusted the Liberal party, they now realize that they have been deceived, and they deeply regret the defeat of the government which was in office from 1957 to 1962.
Mr. Chairman, you will certainly recall that during the 1962 and the 1963 election campaigns, workers were promised a pension scheme without taxation.
That promise was made in all the provinces and it brought votes to the Liberal party. Since the present government has been in power, not only has it introduced a pension plan only to withdraw it later, but it has brought in another scheme, and there is now some talk about a third one.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I wonder how the Liberal party could promise a pension plan during the 1962 and 1963 election campaigns and how it could honestly expect to carry out its pledges.
I have before me a booklet published by the Liberal party during the election campaign, prior to the election held on June 18, 1962. It reads in part:
20220-294J

$140 a month for today's retired couple.
Up to $295 a month when you retire.

And further on, dealing with contributions, it reads as follows:

The Liberal plan will add a contributory pension to the existing old age pension. The addition will be paid for entirely by contributions, not by taxes.
You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that the rate of tax on income has been moved from 3 per cent to 4 per cent. This was to cope with the increase in pension to $75 a month for the old age pensioners. You will also recall, Mr. Chairman, that this increase of $10 a month which was paid to the old age pensioners was implemented only after the official opposition had forced the government to fulfil its promise. Had it not been for the Conservative opposition, as sure as anything the old age pensioners would still be on the $65 a month pension as they were before.

But I would like to prove to the house that the Liberal promises made during the two election campaigns have become dead letters and that those who were supposed to bring such prosperity to the average worker are now unable to fulfil their promises.
I would refer to the two deduction tables with regard to income tax, and particularly forms 101 and 101 A, as well as the one which was introduced in January 1963. If we take as deduction basis a salary of $65 a week, we shall see, for instance, that, for an unmarried person earning $65 a week, the income tax shows a 40 cents increase per week, whereas the married man without dependants, is paying 25 cents a week over and above the amount paid at the time we were in power; the head of a family with two dependant children is paying 50 cents more than under the Conservatives; and a person with four dependant children, 5 cents more a week.
This government made many other promises, which remained just promises. For instance, I wonder why the government is waiting to carry out its promise to create an industrial council. Moreover, during the election campaign, those who are now supporting the government had promised Canadian citizens a special compensation to workers struck by illness. With regard to unemployment insurance, the Liberal party promised, during those elections, to extend

Interim Supply
its benefits to farm workers and, more than a year after the Liberal, have come into power, there is still no sign that farm workers will, in the near future, be covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Another promise which has certainly not been fulfilled is the one I find in the Liberal program of March 1963, and I quote according to this booklet:

The Liberals' objectives for the future are designed to ensure a square deal for labour.
In one of the promises hereafter enunciated we see that a Liberal government would institute a federal labour code, including a minimum wage of $1.25 an hour, a maximum work week of 40 hours, two weeks' vacation and seven statutory holidays. We are still waiting for this.
We are getting close to shore.

The hon. member says we are getting close to shore. We are closer to the end of the world than we have ever been before. The promise leaves us a long way from the shore, just as much as we are a long way from the day when the promise will be fulfilled.
I also see in this pamphlet that the Liberals' policy of economic expansion will restore the unemployment insurance fund and return it to its proper function. It was only a couple of months ago that the fund was drained to the bottom, and if it had not been for some emergency measures the workers of this country would have been deprived of their weekly benefits. Would the hon. member for Levis repeat his remark? I heard what he said though I will not repeat it; but I would have something to tell him if he did repeat it.

All this goes to say that the Canadian people lost confidence in this government long ago.
You will recall, Mr. Chairman, the 1962 election campaign opposed the dollar devaluation. They insisted that such a measure would be detrimental to the Canadian people. According to certain Liberal speakers, a Conservative administration would mean that the Canadian people would head straight for disaster. But, once in power, they forgot to re-establish the dollar parity and carried on where the Conservative party had left off. They even tried to get credit for measures introduced by the Conservative government.

This is not the only thing they had promised. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that they had promised to give Canada a balanced budget. Goodness knows how the budget has been balanced since they are in power. Not only has the budget been in a worse state than ever before, but from one year to the next, we are going from one catastrophe to another, and deficits are piling up.
The Liberals have nevertheless thought they would cure all ills by establishing new taxes. You know as well as I do, Mr. Chairman, that the 11 per cent tax is not extremely popular. It has not been of much help in developing our country. It has momentarily brought money to the government and had it not been for that extra revenue, I wonder what the government would have done.
Not only was 11 per cent tax increased, in addition to the 3 and 4 per cent on income tax, but there was also an increase in postal rates. As you know, the Postmaster General still has a resolution on the order paper to further increase postal rates.
I continually meet middle class people in my riding and I realize that, as a general rule, the people, the ordinary workers, have lost faith in the present Liberal government. I cannot repeat it too often for it is precisely what is happening, and people are anxious to have another opportunity to show their discontent to those who had promised them the moon and stars if they ever came back into power.
We have often been blamed for doing nothing or almost nothing to help the working class. Well, allow me to remind you of some measures which we took when our government was in power and which favoured more particularly what is commonly known as the average citizen.
As soon as we came into office, we amended the Unemployment Insurance Act to make it more consistent with present requirements. For example, we gave married women a status equal to that of the ordinary worker. In 1957, 250,000 workers drew for the first time benefits amounting to $13 million. We changed the periods of seasonal benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act and extended them from 16 to 24 weeks and, in 1958, we extended to 30 weeks the benefits which a worker can draw under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
This favoured 200,000 workers who shared among them an amount of $14 million and, in 1959, we increased the number of weeks for regular unemployment insurance benefits

from 36 to 52 weeks a year. This enabled
80,000	more Canadians to benefit thereby.
What single step did this government take in order to help the working class? It merely continued what the previous Conservative government had established, for which the Liberals are now trying to take credit.
You remember that when the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), who was at that time minister of labour, introduced in the house the legislation intended to help municipalities and the measure concerning winter works, those proposals were greeted with mockery by Liberal members who were then in opposition and who even tried to ridicule them. Those people contended at the time that those measures would not give any practical results. However, if you listen now to their speeches, you realize that they are trying to make us believe that those programs were initiated by them and that they are giving very interesting results.
It is a fact that the results are very interesting and the municipalities are happy to take advantage thereof, but they know however, to whom credit belongs.
For instance, you have the measure concerning sewage treatment plants. Several municipalities have availed themselves of that measure and the results have been excellent and continue to improve constantly, since all the municipalities go on taking advantage of this act, as drinking water supplies are decreasing all the time.
Now, I cannot resume my seat without making a few comparisons in a particular field which concerns more especially the constituency of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. I want to show that this government did not do very much in order to reduce unemployment, especially in the province of Quebec, where we have the sad honour of the greatest number of unemployed in all the provinces of the country.
In the province of Quebec, 112,000 unemployed are looking for jobs. If we refer more especially to the burning speeches made by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), we see that the unemployed, who do not now have a job and are deprived of a salary to support their families, are certainly entitled to expect more from a team which had promised so much, especially in their first 60 days in office.
Indeed, if I refer to a speech made in the house by the hon. member for Essex East, the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, where he promised that the Liberal party would pass a whole series of measures
Interim Supply
if elected, I see that not one of them-except perhaps a half measure-has been implemented to stem unemployment.
Well, I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to read his past speeches over again. I regret he is not in the house, because I would be very happy to remind him of his statements. However, I would ask his colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) or the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) to advise the Secretary of State for External Affairs to read over the speech he made on September 20, 1961, and to convey to his colleague, the Minister of Labour, the information he said he had, so that the latter may take the necessary steps to give work to the unemployed in the province of Quebec.
For over a year, the unemployed in the province of Quebec have been hoping something would be done for them. When we were in power, we were blamed for not doing enough for unemployed workers. If it was wrong at that time to have unemployed people, it is no better now, especially in view of the fact that the province of Quebec alone has at least from 110,000 to 112,000 jobless people. I am asking Liberal hon. members from Quebec who are now in the house to bring pressure to bear on the minister, to discuss the matter in their caucus, in short, to speak for the unemployed. As a matter of fact, it is just as sad to see a man out of work in 1964 as it was in 1962 or 1963.
However, Mr. Chairman, you will recognize that we do not take advantage of human distress as the government members used to do when they were in opposition. In fact, when we were in power, almost not a day went by that the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) or some other Liberal members took the floor to try and make capital out of human distress and to paint a gloomy picture of the lot of Canadian workers.
If government members and more particularly those from Quebec wish to give evidence of honesty, they should work relentlessly on the unemployment problem and discuss it with the Minister of Labour as often as they did when they were in opposition. Only then shall we realize that they were sincere at that time. If they do not follow that course in 1964, it would become clear that their only object was blackmail and that they were not the least interested in the welfare of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I said a while ago that I wished to put on the record some statistics concerning my riding more specifically. I have in my hand some official figures supplied to me by the St. Hyacinthe unemployment insurance office and if I compare the statistics for January, February, March, April and May for the years 1961, 1962, 1963 and 1964, I find that this government did not really try very hard to give employment to unemployed people in Canada.
Thus, in January 1961 at the St. Hyacinthe unemployment insurance office, there were 3,578 unemployed applicants; 2,528 in 1962; 2,543 in 1963 and in 1964, under a Liberal administration, 2,344.
It is falling off.

Mr. Chairman, 1 realize that the figures are decreasing, but it is due to the measures passed by the former Conservative government and which today are bringing results. In fact, I feel compelled to ask, once more, the members of the government to name one single measure taken by this government in order to alleviate unemployment, because I notice that this government continues to apply measures which were all put into effect by the previous government.

Indeed, I would very much like to see the Liberal members, especially those from Quebec, insist on rising as much as they did when they were in opposition.
Including the hon. member for St. Henry.

And I say again that the fact that they do not will prove that they were totally insincere at the time. Indeed, I want to show it beyond any doubt. If my hon. friends opposite feel that the comments I have just made are not in keeping with the facts, let them try and prove it.
In February, 1961, there were 3,919 claimants registered at the St. Hyacinthe unemployment insurance office; 2,613 in February, 1962; 2,700 in February, 1963, and 2,470 in February, 1964.
Now if we look at the number of placements effected during the same period, we note that there were 188 in 1961, 162 in 1962, 208 in 1963 and 231 in 1964. The situation is not too much different from that which prevailed when we were in office. There has been some improvement which, I repeat, is due to the steps we took.
As for the month of February, 139 placements were made in 1961, 177 in 1962, 196 in 1963 and 185 in 1964. There also, there is an advance, but in the opposite direction. I want to draw the attention of the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Cote) to this fact, to spare him the trouble of making rapid calculations.
Mr. Chairman, I do not have time to read the whole table I have here, but it does show rather well what is happening. Far from experiencing, under a Liberal regime, a prosperity beyond compare, Quebec's unemployed are still waiting for something to be done for them, and it is on their behalf that I ask the present government, which had promised full employment, to implement its program.
Mr. Chairman, as I have said, the unemployed in the province of Quebec have been waiting for a solution from this government for more than a year. Surely they will get tired of waiting. Poverty will continue to increase and the blame will lie with the present government which will not have taken necessary steps to prevent that disaster.
Members of the government, set to work. Your turn has come. You have criticized us long enough. Now, it is up to you to show some leadership and to do something for those in need.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make only a few remarks in this debate, which I would say has been a very fine one. Members' contributions to the debate have been useful and helpful. However, if I may say so there were many exaggerations and statements by various members of the opposition which were not entirely in accordance with the facts. It also appears that in this debate members are primarily concerned with the deportation proceedings in regard to individuals who have illegally entered the country. However, it should be understood that the deportation laws have been approved by parliament and are for the protection of the Canadian people. They are administered by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and that department is charged with the responsibility of upholding the laws of this country. I believe that no hon. member would treat lightly the matter of illegal entry into the country. As pointed out by the minister in his statement, he has given an explanation of the elaborate precautions taken to protect the legal and human rights of those who are to be deported. The department goes to great lengths, I might say, to insure that every deportee is furnished with an interpreter whenever necessary, in order to insure reasonable protection for the individuals concerned.
Several instances were brought to my attention in which the minister had personally intervened on the eve of a scheduled deportation and instructed the officials of the department to postpone the deportation to allow further consideration of a case. The Department of Citizenship and Immigration has been charged with the responsibility of increasing Canada's population through immigration, so that we may expand our domestic markets for our agriculture and manufactured products, stimulate economic activity and by providing new skills and ideas to support a higher level of cultural development and cultural independence.
I am sure it is unnecessary for me to remind hon. members of the tremendous responsibilities which the minister and the officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration are facing in carrying out this task. Since the end of world war II, more than two and a half million persons have immigrated to this country. Immigrants today comprise approximately 8.3 per cent of our total population and 12.25 per cent of our labour force. The minister referred also to

the 30 million visitors, tourists and businessmen who cross our borders each year. The importance of these non-immigrants, in terms of good will or economic value to this country, cannot be overemphasized.
This tremendous volume of traffic has been handled efficiently by immigration officers without fuss, without fanfare and with very few complaints. I think they should be congratulated on the job they have done. I repeat these important points only to indicate to hon. members the extent to which the criticisms of some members of this house, in the course of the past few weeks, have reflected in a disproportionate way on the performance of a highly dedicated, hard working group of people. I must confess, and I am sure many hon. members will share my feeling, that I found this regrettable.
Although the number of persons involved in deportations is small in relation to the total number dealt with by immigration officers, the operation of elaborate procedures, the time and effort necessary to deal with them and to protect their human and legal rights are well worth while, as the outline given by the minister has indicated. Parliament has imposed upon the Department of Citizenship and Immigration the responsibility to protect Canada and the people of this country from invasion, if you like, by unsuitable and undesirable elements. The government is anxious that this difficult task should be carried out fairly, with due regard for the protection of the rights of the individual, as well as humanitarian and compassionate considerations.
It is difficult, sometimes, to make generalizations in matters of this kind. However, hon. members can be certain that there is no desire on the part of the minister or the department to act in an arbitrary or tyrannical manner, as suggested by one hon. member this afternoon. I believe it was the hon. member for Bow River who made that assertion. At the same time parliament has placed on the minister and this department the responsibility of exercising a discretion in the granting of admissions. This is not an exercise which the minister takes lightly. While it may not be in the public interest to give an explanation in detail in all situations, as the hon. member for Greenwood has been emphasizing the department should, nevertheless hon. members may take it as a matter of record that a very exhaustive examination of the circumstances is undertaken before a decision is reached.

Apart from deportations, another very important side to this general problem which hon. members might bear in mind is that illegal entrants are not infrequently prohibited persons under the Immigration Act and would be refused a Canadian visa if they applied from another country. By entering Canada illegally as ship deserters, stowaways and non-immigrants, they attempt to obtain priority consideration for their cases, ahead of other more desirable immigrants who follow authorized procedures. They attempt also to obtain priority over the relatives of Canadians who are anxious to be reunited with their families in Canada.
Having said that, I honestly believe that in the light of present day conditions the act, as it now stands, as pointed out by the hon. member for Hamilton West, is inadequate. I hope that when legislation is brought before this house we shall be able to enact some improvements.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona made statements this afternoon about inefficiency and a lack of due regard for the rights of individuals held in custody for illegal entry. I suggest to him that he should read the various exhaustive statements made by the minister in this house, and he will immediately realize that the minister has been more than fair, and any implication to the contrary is not in accordance with the facts.
The hon. member for Royal referred to Greek nationals who enter illegally but who have lived here for four or five years, some of whom have married and have jobs. I might say in this connection that the minister has been lenient in some of these cases and has been instrumental in seeing that landed immigrant status was granted to them.
This I am sure should prove that he is not blind to the humanitarian instincts, and does not hesitate to exercise discretion, giving to many of those who may or may not qualify the benefit of the doubt.
I want to assure the hon. member that this government has not forgotten its promises, nor the intent to gradually develop a progressive immigration policy to fit the times. I sincerely hope, Mr. Chairman, that the members of this committee will bear with the minister and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration to the end that we, in the not too long distant future, will bring about regulations and changes in the act that will be beneficial to the country. Mr. Chairman, I was motivated to participate in this debate by the very vicious and unwarranted attack made by the hon. member for Bow River on the Prime Minister. I think it was a prostitution of the obvious talent of that hon. member that, by using question period statements out of context, he was thus able to turn around and attack a man as great as our Prime Minister.
There are people in this chamber such as the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition who have served the country and the House of Commons well, and I think it is a tragedy in this day and age that people of that stature should be subjected to that type of unwarranted attack, rendered all the more vicious by the fact that the Prime Minister was not present in the chamber at the time.
Read Cardin's speech.

It was pointed out with some accuracy by most hon. members in front of me that it is traditional when making this type of unwarranted attack at least to have the courtesy to notify the person in question about the subject matter in order that he be entitled to refute and answer it. That opportunity was denied the Prime Minister this afternoon.
Check with your Associate Minister of National Defence.

You may make your speech later. I think there is something reverent about leaders of parties, about the positions they fill, and I think that a prime minister

of a country as great as Canada should be free of this type of unwarranted attack, which disgusted most of us here. The Prime Minister has served his country well in war, like many others in this chamber. Later he served this country very well as one of its senior civil servants, and his record as the Canadian delegate to the United Nations is second to none. As the leader of our opposition he did an excellent job.
I know this is a house debate. I know at times the argument gets charged and there are moments when things we say are of a spontaneous nature, but the unfortunate aspect of the attack by the hon. member for Bow River was that it was coldly calculated, and it is little wonder most hon. members on this side feel it was more than a coincidence that this attack on the person of the Prime Minister took place when he was not here to defend himself. I leave it up to hon. members of the committee to say whether or not our Prime Minister has to satisfy hon. members such as the hon. member for Bow River.
People who lie are motivated by fear, and the Prime Minister of Canada has nothing to fear from anybody in this chamber. He has nothing to fear from the film "Mr. Pearson" which I think has occupied a little too much of the time of this house. If the reason the film is being discussed is because of interference with the C.B.C. then I say continue to discuss that matter, because the C.B.C. should not be interfered with by this government or any government, past or future.
But this is not what is happening in our debate. This was not the attack made by the hon. member for Bow River. He was simply using the opportunity, like a jackal chasing deer through the forest, to discredit a man like our Prime Minister; and this is a despicable thing.
