The fourth and final charge to this house in this terrible indictment of the Prime Minister concerned the Olympic games, a matter of national concern. Everyone knows that the minister of health and welfare did attend the winter Olympic games, and the Prime Minister as well as the hon. lady herself so answered when questioned in the house. The confusion, if any exists, lies in the definition as to whether or not we presented a brief on behalf of Banff for the 1968 games. What purpose could the Prime Minister have in misinforming the house on this subject? The facts are very simple. Under the Olympic rules the government could not officially-and I emphasize officially-make representations for the next winter Olympic games since they are awarded to cities, not countries. Whether or not the minister and other officials made unofficial representations on behalf of Banff or on behalf of the country is left for hon. members to decide.
The hon. member for Bow River has made many friends on this side of the house by his very impartial conduct in the privileges and elections committee recently, where he fought hard but fair and square and honestly, and we appreciated his efforts. His aggressiveness remained fair and unsullied, and we would not want to see his reputation tarnished in this house by his unwarranted and unsubstantiated attack on the Prime Minister this afternoon. On reflecting a little I am sure that he, like all hon. members in the house, would not like to take political advantage of a man who has the complete respect of all Canadians. Perhaps the hon. member this afternoon was carried away by the power of his words. He invoked the law of God to strengthen his belief-and these are his words as I saw them later this afternoon-that the Prime Minister should resign. Certainly all hon. members would need not only the law of God but the law of wisdom, the divine law and even the natural law-and he invoked them all-to convince them that the Prime Minister is other than what all hon. members of the house know to be the fact, namely a great Prime Minister, a great Canadian, and a simple, honest, true citizen of Canada.
That was a nice job of whitewash.

Mr. Chairman, I was one of those who were initially interested in this matter of the C.B.C. suppression which this government brought on in respect to the film

"Mr. Pearson", and I have remained interested' in it throughout. I followed the debate on the film and the various questions which were asked, and not only do I think that the hon. member for Bow River was justified in making the remarks he did, which I wholly endorse, but I intend to go further than he did.
After reading Friday's proceedings when hon. members opposite were so thin-skinned as to move a motion to expel the hon. member for Qu'Appelle from the house, I thought to myself that this is a very strange change indeed from the days when the four horsemen of the apocalypse were sitting on this side of the house and charging the then prime minister, who is now the Leader of the Opposition, with gross deceit and other similar epithets to which no objection was raised on the government side at that time.
I am not going to say that the Prime Minister lied; but when reading page 3429 of Hansard we find this answer of the Prime Minister to a question:
-We do not censor films on this side of the house.
I say, sir, that that is a lie, because that is precisely what happened, as I intend to show tonight.
I say too that at page 3430 of Hansard we find a reply of the Prime Minister which is reported as follows:
The circumstances were perfectly proper. The initiative was taken by the producer of the film, and no question of censorship arises.
I also say that that statement is a lie, and I intend to back up my assertions this evening by facts, not by diversionary tactics and flights of fancy such as that embarked upon a moment ago by the hon. member for Verdun.
I submit that all of this points up a pattern which has been forming over the past several months where the government has been using the C.B.C. as a tool for their own propaganda purposes. This has shown itself in a speech which the Minister of Transport made in Quebec city in February of this year; and the Secretary of State, the notable "minister of culture" in this house, has made similar remarks with respect to public communications media. This episode of the film "Mr. Pearson" produced for the C.B.C. at a cost to the Canadian taxpayer of $35,000 is just the culmination of this whole pattern of control which the government is attempting to exercise over the C.B.C. They may have control over the management of the C.B.C. I think, too, this switch from Mr. Dunton to Mr. Oui-met is significant in this regard; it was brought

about shortly after the government now sitting on the treasury benches took office. But while they control the management of the C.B.C., many of the personnel of the corporation's public affairs division do not like this transpiring of events at all. The public affairs personnel I am sure are endeavouring to do a job as impartially as they can and when they receive instructions from top management which in turn receives instructions from cabinet ministers, the Prime Minister, the Prime Minister's secretary and the supreme brain truster of the Prime Minister's office, what can they do? He has a $40,000 a year salary to lose and the other management officials have careers to lose as well. I say that pressures were brought to bear on the C.B.C. in this case and I suggest the facts point indisputably to that conclusion.
I was disappointed in the hon. member for Verdun. I thought he was perhaps overwhelmed by his own press releases which appeared after his contribution to the debate on the flag issue in this house. He almost had us in tears. If it were not for the crocodile nature of his own tears just before supper time he might have made more of an impression on the sensibilities of members of the committee. But, as he said, he is a new member and he was not sitting over here when his party was in opposition, and listening to new lows in the calibre of debate such as that which was exemplified by the Associate Minister of National Defence on one occasion when he made an unpardonable and absolutely rotten attack on the prime minister of Canada. Search as the hon. member for Verdun will, he will not find in any public speech on any public occasion an instance where the leader of the official opposition has had the degrading things to say about the present Prime Minister that the Prime Minister of today had to say about the Leader of the Opposition when he was prime minister of this country. A more degrading exhibition of distortion of the truth which the present Prime Minister was guilty of when he was leader of the opposition could not be found anywhere, and all for the purpose of gaining power, and all for the purpose of deception. If any deception, and to use the present Prime Minister's own words, if any gross deception, existed at that time it existed in the utterances he made at that time with respect to the activity of the then prime minister, now the Leader of the Opposition.
What are the circumstances which have led to an examination of the film "Mr. Pearson"? I believe that pressures were not only brought

to bear by the Secretary of State for External Affairs-that appears to be quite evident- and by the Secretary of State, to whom I am more prone to refer as the minister of culture, since he is in control of every government-controlled medium of information in this country, as well as by the Prime Minister himself, but also by Mr. O'Hagan, the Prime Minister's secretary, and by the supreme brain truster, Mr. Kent, who works in the Prime Minister's office. Absolute nonsense and deception, I say, because apart from the hairsplitting tactics which all the cabinet ministers including the Prime Minister have adopted in respect to the covering up of their snipping and cutting of this film, and their suppression of it and their censorship of it, one fact here emerges: The film was made at a cost of $35,000 to the Canadian taxpayer by a body which is supposed to be independent of any political pressure and yet, mysteriously, for the sole reason, the C.B.C. says, of technical inadequacies, the film is not shown. The hon. member for Verdun has the naivete to say that the pictures which were published, pictures taken inside the cabinet chamber, were not part of the production of the C.B.C. film "Mr. Pearson". Yet in this issue of the Globe and Mail there appeared, obviously clipped out of the film-
At no time did I say they were not in it. I said they did not appear in the film as presently-

At least the hon. member for Verdun has the honesty to rise now and say that there has been clipping and snipping of this film which amounts to censorship, and twist and squirm as hon. members opposite would like, they cannot get around that fact. There is only one member opposite I can think of who could squirm and quiver his way around that fact, and he is the Secretary of State for External Affairs whose fine hand was very prominently displayed in the snipping and cutting which went on.
I asked the Prime Minister on May 21 if the film had been viewed in his office. Instead of being as devious as he was in his replies on that day, he could have said: No, it was not viewed in my office, but I did see it in Toronto. Instead of that he chose not to say anything. He said: It was not seen in my office. Subsequently, under pressure from questioning, he said he had in fact seen it in Toronto. Then, under further pressure, he said he had also seen it in his office in the east block. I asked him if he had seen it five times.
It now transpires that it was viewed on no less than 12 occasions by members of the Prime Minister's cabinet and staff. I believe what I read in the Globe and Mail in this regard. Mr. Braithwaite has obviously made a very careful investigation into these facts. Nobody has denied it. Nobody has denied it over there. The danger exists here that if they viewed it once, if any one of the cabinet ministers or the Prime Minister viewed it once with a view to censoring or snipping any part of it, it was wrong and they know it. What they have done in this whole episode is to prostitute the integrity of the C.B.C. The C.B.C. has no alternative now but to refuse to produce the film. If they do produce it, it will be subject to the pressures brought about by the political connivances of the government, and if they do not produce it the result will be the same. It seems to me that the government is on a very sticky wicket indeed.
What about this right of censorship? When the Prime Minister got back to Toronto from New York where he had a meeting with Mr. Ballentine, Mr. O'Hagan, Mr. Pennebaker and others, the producer drafted a letter to the Prime Minister setting out the conditions he had discussed with the Prime Minister personally. This letter, which Ross McLean of the C.B.C. helped to rewrite into its final version, was an extraordinary document that practically gave the Prime Minister full right

of censorship over the proposed film. At one point it stated:
The finished film will be yours to judge and approve before it is made public and thus will contain nothing to which you object.
Is this objectionable?

In reply to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, may I say that I think it is very objectionable. Surely such a reasonable man, such an intelligent man as the Minister of Trade and Commerce will agree with me-
No, I do not.
-that any letter which would subject any production of the C.B.C. to the right of review is wrong.
If they took a picture of me I would demand it.

This film was contracted to be produced for the C.B.C. with the Canadian taxpayers bearing the cost, and here is Mr. McLean of the C.B.C. agreeing with a state of affairs which became rather uncomfortable for him later on, as I will point out when I have the opportunity. He is agreeing with a policy whereby the producer writes to the Prime Minister and says: You have the right to review the film and anything you wish to object to will be cut out.
Perfectly proper.

Mr. Chairman, if that is the
minister's conception of what is proper, then I think we have no hope for any further independent action on the part of the C.B.C. The minister absolutely astounds me when he says that sort of conduct is perfectly proper. Surely if we are to maintain the integrity of the C.B.C., its actions with regard to what it will produce and what it will not produce cannot be subjected to any action which would in effect constitute a censorship board, whether it be by an individual or by a group such as the cabinet. Surely this is very wrong. The letter did not stop there because Mr. Ballentine agreed to shut off the camera whenever requested to do so. It seems to me that this is going a little bit far if any integrity of independent action on behalf of the C.B.C. is to be maintained.
Finally, he stated he would like to be regarded as a biographer ''as official or unofficial as you desire".
At a later time when the project came under Mr. McLean's control he is reported as having said with regard to the letter:

"We just can't pretend it doesn't exist."... Public affairs supervisor Reeves Haggan wrote to the Prime Minister withdrawing the Ballentine concessions-
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.
Would he himself as a member of the house be prepared to let the C.B.C. do a film on a day in the life of the hon. member for Yukon under the conditions he has now indicated are proper?

I can see no reason why I would not agree completely to the C.B.C. hiring an independent producer like Intervideo Productions to make a film concerning the activities of a day or a month, if they could keep up with me, without any concessions made to me as to what would be kept in that film and what would be taken out of it. There is the nub of the thing. The Prime Minister and his cabinet ministers have had very positive things to say about what will stay in the film and what will be cut out of it, and this is what we on this side say is censorship. This is what is wrong. Belatedly they realized this very thing, because after the letter granting the Prime Minister these concessions had been perused and given a second hard look by the C.B.C. they then repudiated the letter, and after they repudiated it the cutting and snipping still carried on. This is even more astonishing if the minister has been following the events that have transpired because of this fact:
Reeves Haggan wrote to the Prime Minister withdrawing the Ballentine concessions and stating the film would be made according to normal practice, which would be to give the Prime Minister the right to raise certain objections but not permit him to control the film's entire contents.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs apparently came away from the viewing with a long list of objections. Similarly, the Minister of Finance came away from his first viewing of the film with a long list of objections, as did other cabinet ministers. The Secretary of State for External Affairs looks puzzled, so I think I will take him now to the list of objections he raised, in the event that he may want to leave early.
At the screening on January 6, with McLean, Ballentine, O'Hagan and Hal Dornan of the Prime Minister's staff attending, Mr. O'Hagan requested the following sequences be deleted:
A remark by O'Hagan involving Canadian Press.
A remark by the P.M. about a former press secretary of opposition leader Diefenbaker.

An unguarded comment by labour minister Mac-Eachen.
A facetious remark by Mrs. Pearson.
I can remember another facetious remark by Mrs. Pearson that was published in Maclean's magazine just after the last election about the dirty dogs on the prairies.
The prairies will never forget it.

I continue:
Comments by a government chauffeur. One ''Lord'' and two "Gods" by the P.M. (One "heU", one "damn" and one other "God" to be retained.)
Then there is reference to what has come to be familiarly known as the Coutts car sequence. The article continues:
-and some remarks by Gordon Robertson, clerk of the privy council, were discussed, but finally it was agreed the latter would remain. At the conclusion Mr. O'Hagan expressed the opinion that the film was a good one.
What have they left after all these snips and cuts? Usually the Secretary of State for External Affairs is more prominently displayed in the press, but I cannot seem to find him at the moment.
They cut out God.

By April 5 all was settled and Mr. Ballentine screened the finished film for Reeves Haggan. On April 30 he took the print to Ottawa for what was to be the final screening for the Pearson people. This event which took place at the east block office at the fashionable hour of 8 p.m. had some trappings of a major movie opening.
On hand were such luminaries as Keith Davey, president of the National Liberal Federation; Trade Minister Mitchell Sharp; External Affairs Minister Paul Martin (whose comments were to be a highlight) : Tom Kent, supreme brain truster to the Prime Minister; O'Hagan, Reagen, Coutts, Haggan, Ballentine, Dornan and a number of wives and secretaries to the principals. Labour Minister Mac-Eachen arrived about half way through the screening. The Prime Minister wasn't there.
At the final fadeout, Mitchell Sharp described the picture as an "astounding document." Mr. Haggan asked Mr. O'Hagan-
There are a lot of Irish in this.
-if the cut-down Coutts car sequence was okay. Mr. O'Hagan said it was. Paul Martin, who had made notes during the showing, now read these to the happy first night audience, noting his reservations as he went along.
I can just imagine that the reservations of the hon. minister must have been as long as the film itself.

He objected to a portrait of Sir John A. Macdonald in the Prime Minister's office being shown twice while the one of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was never shown.
He objected to the Prime Minister (in the film) referring to Hailie Selassie as the last emperor in the world, since Japan still had an emperor.
As a Roman Catholic, Mr. Martin did not object to the cuss words, but was afraid Presbyterians and Methodists would.
The next bit is understandable, knowing the hon. minister for even the short space of seven years as I have.
Mr. Martin would have gone on, but Mr. O'Hagan suggested that they all go into his office to discuss the film privately, leaving Mr. Ballen-tine outside with Mr. Haggan. Mr. MacEachen stayed with them and they screened for him the part he had missed. He found it highly amusing, as the press gallery reporters would when they saw it much later.
In about half an hour, Mr. Ballentine and Mr. Haggan were called to Mr. O'Hagan's office, where they were told that everyone thought highly of the film. Tom Kent called it brilliant. However, it must be understood that there was some concern about it from a publicity and political point of view.
Mr. Haggan said he thought it was sympathetic to the Prime Minister. But some of the Liberals were afraid it might not be understood by the public, that it might too confusing. Anyhow, Mr. O'Hagan said, there could be no decision right then because the matter had to be discussed with the Prime Minister.
Possibly it is reasonable, sir, to wonder whether Mr. Ballentine's offer to the C.B.C. over the film rights had not coloured his attitude considering the almost incredible concessions he made to the Prime Minister in his letter of September 23. It is almost inconceivable that such concessions could be made which would so prostitute a government crown corporation charged with the responsibility of independently and impartially disseminating public information. To have made such a concession, I think, is gross control and, in fact, censorship. The main point of the C.B.C. was to conduct a private screening for the Prime Minister and his aides of the film that was later to be shown to the public as a candid documentary, independently made and not an official government or Liberal party film.
Here, I would suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce is the distinction between his assertion that these concessions were perfectly proper, the distinction between that sort of attitude which, in effect, I suggest to him amounts to absolute censorship of a production by the C.B.C., something to which the C.B.C. should not be subjected to at all, and the situation where the Liberal party may have had a film made which they could review, snip and cut to their hearts' content. However, in this situation, the propriety of the

corporation's accommodating attitude and action is open to question.
I say it is open to question, and this is one of the reasons that the government is in such a dilemma now. If the C.B.C. does submit to the pressures that are brought and continues to refuse to show the film, then you have a situation where the government is, in effect, controlling broadcasting. On the other hand, the integrity of the C.B.C. management cannot be the same at all because if they do show the film the only reason they will change or alter their decision will be the political implications that have arisen out of the fumbling and bumbling of the government in its handling of this whole issue. What we have in this situation is a crown corporation responsible to a political party, the Liberal party. What we have in this situation is a crown corporation, which is supposed to be independent and which has been subjected to political control, censorship and political pressure by the government in office.
I well remember how the present Minister of Transport, when he was on this side of the house, rose in his righteous wrath and indignation at the time of the suspension of the production "Capital Report". I can still hear him waxing eloquently on the independence of the C.B.C. Where has that independence gone today? It has been completely suppressed by the actions of the government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, I regret that I have to advise the hon. member that his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, the committee has had, I think, far too much of the Pearson film. I think the responsibility, in the main, rests on the fact that the whole matter has been bungled, I will not say by the government, but obviously by the coterie within the Prime Minister's office. On the whole, I think they have been less than candid.
I should like to begin my remarks with what is, in effect, an apology. In looking at Hansard I see the Prime Minister challenged me during the question period to indicate whether I had any evidence to prove there was actually a formal cabinet meeting or a formal meeting of the subcommittee of cabinet for the film, since I had seen the film. I had hoped that I had not tried to give that impression. Certainly, I was aware that this was a meeting of cabinet ministers. It was obvious that there was not an official there from the privy council office to give it any official sanction.
However, I should like to make one particular point in connection with this matter.

The real power, as is so often the case in a Canadian situation, is in the shadow or ceremonial imprimatur that cloaks reality and is a myth not in things such as an official cabinet meeting, a subcommittee of the cabinet, and so on. The reality is that we were given in that film something a little more racey than a subcommittee meeting. We were actually seeing an ad hoc group of ministers meeting with the Prime Minister to discuss an issue of the day. It is obviously not an official cabinet meeting nor an official subcommittee meeting of the cabinet, but I would suggest it is not semantic to argue that the impression of the real reality was that this was an important meeting.
I do not know whether these things should have been exposed to film or not, but I just want to present that as a bit of an addendum to the discussion which took place here when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle was named. There is a hypothesis I want to put before the committee. I do not think we will ever get the true and exact story of what took place. I have spoken at length to the official spokesman of the C.B.C. about this and questioned him about it. I refer to Ron Fraser, vice president of the C.B.C.
I have known Mr. Ballentine for some years and have been acquainted with his whole position, and I believe Dennis Braithwaite of the Globe and Mail was almost completely indebted for the details in this column, that was read by the hon. member for Yukon, to Mr. Ballentine. Also, like many other members around here I have other contacts through which information comes to me and I think I can reconstruct almost everything that took place. There is very little that took place that is not in the Braithwaite story, but the whole key of the issue is: Was there political interference?
My hypothesis-and of course it depends how you look at it-is that there was. I honestly believe that at this meeting where the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Trade and Commerce buttered up Mr. Ballentine a little bit after seeing the film, and then withdrew into their private discussions-I honestly believe that the decision was taken there that this film should not run. I honestly believe that from what I know, and my hypothesis is that the vote was overwhelmingly that the film should not run.
I also believe that Mr. Haggan was privy to this decision at this very point, and I think Mr. Haggan, from the views set out in Mr. Braithwaite's article, was prepared
Interim Supply
to fight against this, but I think in honesty to his own superiors I should point out and remind hon. members that here is the director of the public affairs programming of C.B.C. television, repeatedly in on these discussions. In other words he recognized this was a very important and difficult film, and he had close contact throughout. I am convinced, and I advance it as my hypothesis, that Mr. Haggan was aware, either through Mr. Richard O'Hagan, the press secretary, or through some closer contact with the people who took the vote, that it was the feeling of the government that this film should not be shown, and it is my hypothesis that he submitted this opinion to his superiors; but I think he wanted to show it despite what they felt.
But I think once that view was given to his superiors about the way the cabinet ministers, and the particular little coterie that hangs around the Prime Minister's office and assists as his advisers on things like that, felt-once that happened, this led the officials to make their decision. Obviously the idea of the Prime Minister picking up the phone and calling Mr. Ouimet or Mr. Fraser and saying, "We don't want that to run" did not happen. I think it is nonsense to suggest that.
I am not suggesting there was anything particularly devious or dirty about what took place, but certainly that vote of the Liberals against the film somehow got to the senior people of the C.B.C. and I think this influenced their judgment, along with the fact that some of them were against what they called the technical shortcomings of the film. That is my hypothesis and I do not know where we go from here.
I suggest one of the reasons this situation developed is because typically this government and this Prime Minister continue to be less than candid with the House of Commons and with the people. I am not suggesting the members of the government are deliberately dishonest, but they are managerial. They are trying to manipulate, and I want to offer evidence of this. A lot of hon. members have not seen the film but I want to mention two incidents in the film which indicate the kind of managerial approach I am talking about.
There is a little discussion in the film, at least in the film I saw down at Crawleys, about a telecast the Prime Minister is going to do the next day, and it is very entertaining to watch the sort of Uriah Heap-ish mothering that Tom Kent gives him. He is going to make sure he has everything lined up for the telecast, but in that discussion that takes place, with Mr. Kent's unction flowing

Interim Supply
around the scene, there is a suggestion that the Leader of the Opposition would demand equal time. The Prime Minister says, "We are not going to have any of that," or words to that effect. It is right there in the film itself but no one has picked it out and selected it as an indication of the approach I am talking about. There is the suggestion, "No, we are going to handle this thing so that the Leader of the Opposition is not going to have a go."
It illustrates something it is hard for me to understand-the inordinate fear the Prime Minister has of the former prime minister; but it also indicates the approach, "We are going to manage things so that we are going to have things our way. We are going to have the image, not them."
The other point is also a compelling one. The Minister of Labour is interviewed by Mr. Harnett of CFRB, a radio man here on parliament hill. The minister gets into a predicament in this scene and I sympathize with him because I have encountered it myself on occasion. He gets into this predicament and says too much about the fact that it may be necessary to call troops in on the Montreal dockers' strike. Then he starts up the stairs- a beautiful scene-then turns back and says, "I would appreciate it very much if you did not run that little bit," and the reporter, Mr. Harnett, says, "You want it cut out"? and the minister says, "I would really appreciate it." Well, a minister of the crown asks you to do something like that. Fine. There is nothing really wicked, but I suggest to you it is part of the managerial approach-"we know how to govern; we know how to manage things," and one of the great problems of the government across the way is that this approach is really their downfall.
They think they are the administrative geniuses. They think they know how to handle things, but ever since they got in they flubbed on point after point. These people are manipulators. They think they can manage and think they can do things, and though I do not feel sorry I do feel sympathy for a lot of the government backbenchers who have to sit there and watch the finicky perambulations along the front bench, as they watch one minister after another getting into trouble, right from the budget of last year down to this last and silliest of things.
Can you imagine the amount of time parliament has taken up with this ruddy television film? Yes, I have helped to bring that about because it is a classic example of the approach of this government. They don't like criticism. They cannot stand it. They have not got the

skin for it. When they were over here we used to call them the four horsemen of the apocalypse. You could not stop them; they were in there knifing. But once they got into power they wanted to get back to those pre-1957 days, warm, with Blair Fraser putting out the honeyed phrases about this greatest collection of talent in Canadian history. Haw, haw, haw.
Here we have a situation that could have been cleared up right off by a candid, complete statement of about 200 words by the Prime Minister. But instead, what happened- they backed away and backed away, and the terrible thing is that one television man's reputation, Mr. Ballentine's reputation, could have been ruined. Maybe it is ruined over this incident, but not one of the ministers in this particular case was prepared to come to the rescue.
What does the Secretary of State for External Affairs tell us? He rebuffed me and there was this big laugh. This was his private life; why should anybody interfere with his private life? He told this producer he was pretty good. Tom Kent thought this was a brilliant documentary. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, what was his approach-"an astounding documentary". He told this producer he had done a good job. Yet where were they when it came to standing up for this man who had been insulted by the C.B.C.? This is the kind of thing I think is important. Where is your heart, I say to them, when someone's whole career is put in jeopardy? Where are you? You saw the film; you did not like it; you handed out a bit of blarney, and then you turned around and let the fellow sink. This is one of the tragic things about it, this managerial nonsense about the crew.
This is an excellent television film and it would not do the Prime Minister one bit of harm. As a matter of fact, I think it would show him to a great many people in this country in a sympathetic light. But they are so smart-alecky, so managerial, so much the image-makers that they just could not let it go through; they could not take the chance. This is a government that, as a result of one tawdry little incident, have lost sight of the fact that they have blighted one man's reputation and have put the C.B.C.'s integrity in jeopardy. Yet the Prime Minister the other day told us, "Wait till interim supply and I will have a statement". What do we get? I mean no insult to the hon. member for Verdun, but that hon. member comes in, in reply to an attack made by the hon. member for Bow River, and reads a speech that I

suggest he must have had some advice on from certain quarters.
Hear, hear.
I do not object to that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I am sure that the hon. member, who was not in the house when the hon. member for Verdun first rose, would not want to mislead the committee. The hon. member for Verdun was here and started to speak immediately he had the opportunity.

I am not a sensitive soul like the crew over there or the crew here; I am not making an accusation. If the hon. member for Verdun thinks this Prime Minister is a great Prime Minister and he has been unfairly attacked, more power to him in getting up and defending him. But where is the Prime Minister? He undertook last week that he would be here. I am not suggesting that he can be here all the time, but he should have come here on interim supply and given us the full story, because it appears that his spokesman on radio and television matters, the Secretary of State, knows nothing about it in fact; he knows nothing about this story because he was excluded, really, from the developments.
The quiet man.
Quieter than you, anyway.

I am not trying to be unfair to him; but the whole point is that there was this small group centred in the Prime Minister's office who wanted to turn out something that would be really terrific, and when they found out it was not really terrific, then we get the squeeze, then we get the pressure, then we get the clamp.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this house should forget about this incident in any detail as soon as we get a statement from the Prime Minister or someone who is authorized to speak for him, and who can set out the thing from the beginning to the end from the government's point of view. Then let us have some kind of solution initiated by the government, about which I am sure spokesmen for the parties in the house are prepared to agree, and have indicated to the C.B.C. that this film must and will be shown. I want to suggest to hon. members that when the film is shown everyone will wonder what all the panic was about. This is to my mind, despite what the hon. member for York-Humber said about it, a rather brilliant film. I think the conception of starting with a radio broadcast
Interim Supply
in the morning and ending with the national news at night, with the voice of Earl Cameron blending all the way through, is a very good idea. There is the deliberate denial of a great deal of editing or pushing by any announcer to tell you what is going on. This is part of the success of the film. But this is a matter of individual judgment.
One of the things I find it hard to forgive the C.B.C. for is the excuse that this film had technical shortcomings and was not up to normal standard. This really hurt me, because I was on a C.B.C. program last year that, frankly, was a turkey; it was one of the real lousy stinkers the C.B.C. has turned out. It was an hour program. I can still remember it when they talk of technical shortcomings. For about two minutes there was the voice of John Deutsch, the head of the economic council, I think, over the film with the view of the Ottawa river sparkling in the sunlight. This is what you get when you talk about the technical standards of some of the C.B.C. programs. There was another long shot in the program. I remember that the band was playing "Chicago, Chicago" and we had a view of some skyscrapers silhouetted against the sky. And it was supposed to be a program on university education. I saw this three times while waiting for the show to go on, and I could not figure out what it was doing there. But this is in reference to the C.B.C.'s idea of technical excellence.
I would like to suggest to the minister who answers for the C.B.C. that we have had a little bit too much of this technical shortcomings aspect of the matter. We had the film about the advertising agency and the beauty product by Kelly that was withdrawn because it did not come up to technical standards. We have had a film on "Toronto File" of a young lady who had some unfortunate adventures, and that has not been shown because supposedly it is not technically good enough. This technical difficulty may be an indication of the high standards of the C.B.C., but I would like to suggest they would be much better giving us some more direct and thorough answer and reasons, particularly in connection with the "Mr. Pearson" film.
The last point I wanted to make, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the Pearson film returns to this whole question of the managerial approach this government seems to have to news, news management and to its image. This terrible sensitivity of the government to criticism is a complete denial of the tactics that government members themselves used when they were in opposition. Surely they

Interim Supply
do not think they can go back to the good old pre-pipe line days when the sun shone in the sky, C. D. Howe was right with the world and the Liberals were wonderful. They cannot go back to that, and it is about time they faced up to the fact that maybe some of the criticism that is coming their way is merited and worth while. I cannot think of a better challenge to government backbenchers than to read what the hon. member for Bow River said in his indictment. Not that I support it all the way down the line. They should read it to see the number of times and the indications of prevarication, half truth or just a part of the truth. I do not say it is lying, Mr. Chairman, but I do say there is so much of it; so many of these inconsistencies.
I think of the comment of Charles Lynch of Southam News Services the other day about the capacity of the government. One of the things he had to say about the Diefen-baker government was, "They were never really clever or sharp enough to cover up their mistakes". He said about the present government, "It is using all its cleverness and sharpness to cover up its mistakes". I suggest this is the perfect incident that symbolizes the effect that has become so apparent in this government. I would like to suggest it is about time the Prime Minister or those who have some influence with him began to seize upon some opportunities to be honest and direct in all the dealings they have with this house and with the country.
Hear, hear; it's about time.

Let us put the challenge to this government that has so much conceit and has done so little to deserve its own conceit, that from now on in their dealings with the House of Commons and with the country they stop speaking either out of only one side of their mouth or telling only one part of the truth. As someone in my own constituency said after the Prime Minister appeared on one of his television interviews a few months ago, "One thing you have to say about him, he will admit his mistakes". I am not suggesting that we have the whole confessional here, but I would suggest that the cabinet and the Prime Minister had better be a little more candid and deal a little more quickly with their mistakes. Then perhaps they will have some effect in this country and in this house and will begin to move toward all the claims which hon. members are making for them.

Mr. Chairman, in the last speeches made in this house by the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for Port Arthur, and earlier today by the hon. member for Bow River, serious charges have been made. There has been documentation of deceit resembling half truths and deviousness of the worst kind. Thus we have come at this hour to suggest to the Prime Minister and to the members of the government that it would not be enough to come to the house and admit their error or to apologize. I think it has gone far beyond that. We require one thing and one thing only, and that is that if these charges are correct-and they have not been denied; the documentation is so complete that they could not be denied-we must have some resignations.
Oh, oh.

We
have had documentation of half truths, incomplete explanations, devious explanations, false explanations, no explanation. What is the tradition of parliament if we do not demand resignations? When a government is found guilty of these things, as this government has been, there must follow the resignations of those who are responsible; and if the backbench members of the government understand their position and the situation the government is in, they will demand the resignation of those who have led them into such a situation.
What is involved here, and let there be no mistake about it, is censorship; the total and complete control of the major public communications medium in this country. It is possible to become emotionally involved in this, and perhaps I am speaking with heat, but I have the right to do so. I have sat in this house this afternoon and again this evening listening to hon. members making charges against the government more serious than those which were made of any government since the Liberal government of 1956. Yet there has been total silence and no defence. There can be no defence possible of an indefensible position.
What has been the consequence of this? The Canadian people have made their judgment on that, and perhaps the last court of appeal will again be the Canadian people. But there ought to be in the party which now forms the government, a party with a great tradition behind it, sufficient strength among its backbenchers to demand the truth, not

just for parliament but for the people of Canada, about the censorship of the principal medium of communication in Canada. This is no time for playing or for making lighthearted decisions. We have been altogether too kind on this side of the house in asking for some kind of explanation from the Prime Minister. It is too late for explanations. It is too late even now for the truth from the Prime Minister, the complete and total truth, the whole story. This has had to be dragged out, not here on the floor of the house but by newspaper articles which are undenied, and from other sources of information unchallenged. We on the opposition side of the house challenge the government side that we not only require the total truth but we also require the resignations of those who have misled this house and given the house less than the truth in the last several weeks. There is no other answer to the charge. If there is, let anyone who can suggest it get up and challenge me now.
And let them not hide outside this house.
I have said, Mr. Chairman, if there is anyone on the government side who wishes to challenge my position now, I will yield him the floor.
They haven't got the guts.

But
they do not. Our position is that we have read the story in the Globe and Mail. We have heard the accusations which have been made by a number of speakers on this side of the house. It seems quite apparent that this film was subjected to scrutiny both by the cabinet and by the government. It was never shown. I do not think there has ever been an occasion since the founding of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation where a film of this kind was made ostensibly for the members of the cabinet of the government of the day, and then withdrawn and refused to the public of Canada. There is no question that, whether or not it was a deliberate censorship, it was censorship in fact, because the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and many other senior ministers expressed dissatisfaction with, or less than enthusiasm for, the film. This became very apparent to those who headed this public corporation, which is supposed to come under the jurisdiction of parliament but which in fact has now been debased and comes under the influence of the government itself. There is no
Interim Supply
precedent for this in Canada. There is no justification for what has taken place. Therefore my suggestion to the government is that those who are responsible for this censorship must resign, and they must resign at once.
Mr. Chairman, it seems a shame that no one on the front benches of the government will rise in his place and defend the Prime Minister of the day.
They cannot do it.

And defend the cabinet ministers who saw the preview of the film. It is a shame, and once again I am thankful that I do not belong to a party which is so gutless that they allow three or four speakers in a row to accuse them of lying, accuse them of deviation, of half truths, and not one of them will rise in his place to defend the cabinet members or the Prime Minister. I call them "gutless wonders", and that includes the cabinet and the gutless bunch of backbenchers over there.
I sat in my seat and gave these people time to rise and defend themselves. But shame on them; they would not.
They cannot.

I only accept their silence as an admission that they are guilty. The hon. member for Yukon, the hon. member for Port Arthur and the hon. member for Bow River, who spoke this afternoon, laid the facts bare and there was no defence or denial.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No answer, nothing.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce was in the house and made some halfhearted attempts to answer the hon. member for Yukon when he was speaking. He said that censorship was all right when it concerned the Prime Minister; at least that is what I understood him to say. I am sure Castro would agree with him. I am sure Khrushchev would agree with him. But why did he not remain in the house and set the record straight? Why did he not rise in his place when the hon. member for Yukon had finished and say: "I never saw the film and I deny I voted either for or against it". He left the house because he knew that if he remained in his seat he would have to rise and make some sort of an attempt to answer the accusations made. In fact, when I look at the front benches now I see very few of the ministers who were in on the 12 previews. Why are not some of them in

Interim Supply
the chamber-some of those who saw the film? It is because they do not want to answer the charges which have been made tonight. That is the nub of it, as far as I can see.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: May I ask a question? Does the hon. member not think that the reason these ministers are not in the house may be that they have judged the calibre of the back benches of the opposition parties who are making these filthy smear charges?
You are learning arrogance quickly.

I have ripped up and down the cabinet and the back benches and finally provoked a weak effort to smear me and fellow members who have spoken on this side of the house. But there has been no defence-no answer to the accusations which have been made. There has only been this weak attempt to smear previous speakers by those who feel they rule by divine right, as the hon. member for Port Arthur said- by those who feel that through proper management they can create and project an image which will never be forgotten by the Canadian people and which will keep them in their places forever and a day.
The Canadian people are not so gullible. They will not stand for a minister who has jurisdiction over the C.B.C but who fails to rise to defend the C.B.C. when charges are made. He does not care. I have never seen a minister in this house fail to come to the defence of his department or of the civil servants for whom he is responsible. I have never seen that happen before in my six years in parliament. But tonight accusations have been made and the minister has failed to defend the people involved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members are aware, the automotive program introduced on November 1, 1963 was designed to bring about a rationalization, to some extent, of the automobile and parts industries and to encourage efficient production. These measures provide for the conditional removal of import duties on automobiles and parts and do not involve a grant or bounty.
It is public knowledge that at least six months ago and probably longer the United States treasury department received a petition from the Modine Manufacturing Company of the United States in respect of radiators shipped from Canada to the United States. Under the terms of section 303 of the United States tariff act the U.S. treasury has referred this for investigation, as they must do, to the bureau of customs.
The Canadian government has made representations to the United States in connection with this whole matter and has pointed out that we attach the greatest possible importance to this policy, which is designed not only to provide jobs all through this country in our manufacturing industries, and is doing it, but is designed to increase our exports to the United States and in this way reduce our balance of payments. I think I can say we expect great things from this policy and I can assure the hon. member that we have been bringing and will continue to bring the strongest pressure on our American friends to make sure it is not interfered with. In this connection we have had conversations with the United States government both in Washington and here, and last week end I also had the opportunity of a discussion with Secretary Dillon in Paris. This matter is being pressed 

by the government most energetically and I can assure the hon. member that we consider, as he does, that it is a very urgent matter and one which is most important for the future of this country.

subtopic: FORT WILLIAM, ONT.- REPORTED SEGREGATION OF STUDENTS
FORT WILLIAM, ONT.- REPORTED SEGREGATION OF STUDENTS
speechtext:
This afternoon I directed a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration having to do with news items which appeared in the press a week or more ago to the effect that, in a school in Fort William, Indian students were being segregated from the rest of the students.
People all across Canada and members of all parties have been and are concerned about the plight of the Indian population of Canada and the steps taken to improve their condition. One of the most important of these steps in the long run was the decision of the department that whenever possible Indian children attending school should have the opportunity to attend the regular school attended by students drawn from the population as a whole. It was therefore disturbing to read reports of a conference held in Kenora, Ontario, a couple of weeks ago sponsored by the Indian-Eskimo association and attended by representatives of government and various agencies interested in the problems and rights of the Indians at which it was alleged that Indians from a reserve attending one school in Fort William were segregated. There was subsequent report that there is no segregation of the students in classes. Then it was suggested there was some segregation in the play facilities. Later it was explained that there was segregation in the lunch room.
I will be the first to recognize the fact that there may be difficulties. If, for example, certain students are slow learners, then whether they be Indians or anybody else, if the education authorities think that they can best be educated in special classes, then I for one would have no objection. Similarly I would have no objection to people who were physically handicapped, for instance, having their own play facilities. But I think it would be completely wrong if Indian students attending a school in Fort William or anywhere else had to eat their lunches completely separated from the other students. If it is suggested, for example, that the students are rowdy or difficult, maybe that is a legitimate reason for some kind of separation, but let it include all students who are rowdy

or difficult to handle. I would hope that the department would not countenance segregation in total or in part.
That is all I wanted to inquire about this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that the minister's representative will be able to assure me and the house that the department does not and will not countenance any type of segregation against any minority group, whether it be Indians or anybody else.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hubert Badanai (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: FORT WILLIAM, ONT.- REPORTED SEGREGATION OF STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the officials of the Indian affairs branch, on seeing the newspaper articles referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), got in touch with the school authorities in question and have received assurances from them that there is no segregation. I want to assure the hon. member that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, which has jurisdiction over Indian affairs, is in full agree-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion ment with total integration and we certainly do not countenance segregation at any time.
The allegation made at a meeting in Ken-ora, Ontario, referred to by the hon. member, was to the effect that Indians were taught in the same building as white children but ate in separate rooms and were not integrated on the playground. I understand that a meeting called by the separate school board of Fort William, will be held for the purpose of investigating these allegations. As soon as we receive information as to the result of the meeting I will communicate the information to the hon. member.
Again I want to assure him and all other hon. members that there is no intention on the part of the Indian affairs branch to countenance anything having to do with segregation. We believe in integration, particularly of the children in our public schools.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.20 p.m.
